items.prompt: Explain how a better layout can improve Nera’s labour productivity. Nera Assembly loses time walking between distant storage and workstations. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Productivity can improve through relevant skills, suitable technology, better layout, maintenance, reliable inputs, motivation and effective coordination. Trace the mechanism: less time waiting for materials can increase acceptable output per hour; fewer defects can increase usable output from the same input. Training can be on-the-job or off-the-job according to need and available expertise. An improvement requires actual use and suitable conditions, not simply buying a machine or announcing a target. Extra output achieved solely by proportionately extra hours is not a productivity gain. A practical layout change can reduce handling time and increase acceptable units per labour hour without asking for longer shifts. Check safety and quality so the faster process does not merely create defects.
marking_guidance: Starting point: Productivity can improve through relevant skills, suitable technology, better layout, maintenance, reliable inputs, motivation and effective coordination.

items.prompt: Explain how illness-related absence can affect output and why a supportive response matters. A workshop faces periods of illness-related absence and care demands affecting some staff; no assumption is made about any individual’s diagnosis or capability. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Illness associated with HIV and AIDS can affect attendance, working capacity, skills continuity and household care demands, potentially disrupting output and raising replacement costs. Effects vary; HIV status alone does not establish that a person cannot work. Support, confidentiality, non-discrimination and access to appropriate prevention, care and treatment services matter. Stigma can damage cooperation and discourage seeking support. Discuss the business mechanisms conditionally rather than label all affected people unproductive. This is a workplace-impact lesson, not medical advice or a reason to exclude workers. The ILO emphasises care, support and non-discrimination in its [workplace code](https://www.ilo.org/publications/ilo-code-practice-hivaids-and-world-work). Absences can interrupt a task sequence and create a need for cover. Cross-skilling and supportive arrangements can reduce disruption while protecting dignity; blaming or excluding people based on perceived status can worsen relationships.

items.prompt: Distinguish between the three stated production sequences. Omi Furniture makes one customised cabinet; Kena Bakery makes groups of different loaf types; Hila Bottles operates a continuous standard bottling line. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Job production makes a single product at a time, usually to the customer’s exact specification. Batch production makes a group of similar units before changing to another group. Flow production moves standardised units through a continuous sequence of stages. Compare volume, variety and sequence: customised one-off work differs from repeated groups and from a continuously operating standard line. Job production can offer flexibility with high skill and time per unit; batches balance variety and repetition but require changeovers; flow can support high volume but needs dependable demand, coordination and equipment. A flow line does not guarantee lower unit cost if capacity is underused or coordination and breakdown costs offset savings. These respectively illustrate job, batch and flow. The product’s name alone does not determine the method; describe how the stated process handles units.
marking_guidance: Difference: Job production makes a single product at a time, usually to the customer’s exact specification.

items.prompt: Explain how purchasing savings and coordination problems can affect Hena’s average cost as it expands. Hena Packs can negotiate a material discount for larger orders, but rapid expansion also creates stock-control errors. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Scale of operation concerns the size or capacity of business activity. Economies of scale are causes of average-cost reductions as scale increases, such as purchasing advantages, use of specialist equipment or management and spreading suitable fixed costs across more output. Economies of scale lower average cost only when output actually increases and the extra capacity is used. Diseconomies can arise at the same time, so the overall average cost of a growing business may not fall if they cancel out the savings. Diseconomies are causes of average-cost increases beyond a scale, for example communication difficulties, slower decisions or reduced coordination. Total cost can rise while average cost falls, so keep the measures distinct. This concerns business costs, not the economy’s system of ownership and resource allocation. The discount can reduce unit cost if useful sales justify the larger purchase and storage and coordination costs do not offset it. The errors can create diseconomies, so growth is not automatic evidence of lower average cost.

items.prompt:
Nara Cabinets receives varied custom orders requiring local measurement. It has skilled workers and suitable local premises. It compares job production near customers with a distant standard flow line whose lower stated rent is offset by slow customer contact. For part (b) only, demand changes to a dependable large contract for identical cabinets delivered on a non-urgent schedule; individual local measurement is no longer required. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate Nara’s method and site combination under the original facts. [12]
b Evaluate it after demand changes to the stated standard contract. Explain whether the recommendation should change. [12]
items.canonical_answer: a Local job production matches individual specifications and measurement access. A distant standard line does not solve those needs and may sit underused; lower rent is insufficient. Prefer local flexibility despite its labour requirement. b The standard non-urgent contract removes individual measurement and strengthens the case for flow at a suitable site. Because the contract is for a fixed quantity, batch production of the identical cabinets may give most of the repetition savings without committing to a continuous flow line; flow is justified only if similar large orders are expected to continue. Dependable volume can use capacity, though coordination, breakdown and other diseconomies may offset expected unit savings. Distance is less harmful when delivery is not urgent, but compare transport, equipment investment, skills and contract duration before moving. The original method preference weakens; investigate flow and the alternative site rather than approve automatically. The decision changes with volume, variety and access needs, not with a universal ranking of methods.
